task.implemented: Landed by grok via merge-train; reviewer-approved (run run-1784511918221-3e50ab9e, b23554754bad84318cbffb0df3c675da625ff124).

task.title: Close the post-land CHANGELOG gap: no workflow step owns writing entries
acceptance_criteria: A landed task without a CHANGELOG entry is mechanically detectable, and the detection runs somewhere that surfaces it (check command, audit step, or dashboard fact) rather than depending on someone remembering
Ownership of writing the entry is assigned to exactly one step in the loop and documented in priv/includes/harness-workflow.md and skills/harness-driver/SKILL.md; sync script run
The chosen mechanism does not reintroduce the write-set collision Task 367 closed: reviewers still never edit CHANGELOG.md inside a run worktree
No keyword classifier or prose-quality heuristic in harness code - section placement and wording either come from an agent or from a fact harness already holds
Backfill is not re-litigated: the twelve entries written by the 2865076 audit stand as-is
Tests cover the detector against a landed-task-with-entry and landed-task-without-entry fixture
out_of_scope: Rewriting or restyling existing CHANGELOG history
Generating release notes or version cutting
Changing how the lander advances task status (done --shipped-in stays)
task.body:
Twelve consecutive landed tasks (332, 335, 336, 337, 338, 353, 357, 365, 367, 368, 369, 370) shipped with zero CHANGELOG entries; the last documented task was 352. The post-merge audit for range 2865076 wrote all twelve entries by hand as a fix-forward, which is the symptom, not the fix.

Root cause: no step in the implement -> review -> land loop owns the CHANGELOG. Task 367 deliberately excluded CHANGELOG.md from delivery commits (so a reviewer filing from a stale fork cannot collide on it) and explicitly listed "CHANGELOG generation from verdicts" as out_of_scope. The orchestrator was left as the implicit owner, and in practice it does not do it - the gap ran twelve tasks deep before an audit caught it.

Decide where the ownership lands and make it structural rather than a convention nobody executes. Candidate seams, in rough preference order: (a) the lander writes an entry from the verdict/task metadata as part of the same writeback that already does `done --shipped-in`; (b) the post-merge audit agent owns it as a standing responsibility with a check that fails when a landed task has no entry; (c) an explicit orchestrator step with a mechanical detector so the omission is loud.

Note the mantra constraint: harness may mechanically assemble an entry from facts it already holds (task title, id, shipped sha, acceptance criteria), but it must not judge prose quality or classify an entry into Added/Changed/Fixed by keyword regex. If the entry needs authored prose, an agent writes it; harness only counts and detects the absence.

SUPERSEDED 2026-07-29 (roadmap review): contradicts the canonical CHANGELOG policy (task-prioritization.md: "CHANGELOG.md is release notes, not a task archive... No per-task entries"). A per-task-entry detector mechanizes the wrong invariant — the 12-entry audit backfill was itself the policy violation, not the gap. Release-worthiness is orchestrator judgment at release time; no replacement task filed.

task.title: Persist witness events as a shared, queryable human+agent timeline
acceptance_criteria: A Notification sink persists every fired Event to Postgres (schema + migration) when repo_enabled: true; repo_enabled: false degrades to the store-convention ephemeral fallback, never a file
The sink remains read-only by construction (Sink behaviour grants no merge capability); absent config stays a silent no-op; existing FileSink/CommandSink behavior is unchanged
An api()-annotated MCP query tool (Manifest-registered) lists/filters persisted events by project, run_id, event type, and time range — params MCP-JSON-expressible only (strings / ISO8601)
No judgment in code: the surface relays persisted facts verbatim — no classification, scoring, or filtering-by-importance
Tests: persistence round-trip per event type, query filters, no-op when unconfigured, ephemeral fallback when repo is disabled
out_of_scope: Nostr/Buzz relay integration — no Buzz deployment exists; this is the harness-native timeline (a relay sink would be a later additive Sink implementation)
A dashboard timeline panel — separate surface; the MCP/read API is the deliverable here
Per-event filtering/importance rules or any event classification
task.body:
Inspired by Block's Buzz (https://github.com/block/buzz): a unified event log where humans and agents share one searchable timeline of everything that happened. Harness already counts the facts — Harness.Notification fires Event structs (landed / blocked / post_merge_red / in_run_discernment / persist_failed) to configured sinks — but delivery is fire-and-forget: FileSink appends jsonl, CommandSink execs a command, and no durable queryable store exists (verified: lib/harness/notification/ holds only event/sink/file_sink/command_sink). Orchestrator agents tail ~/.harness/settled.jsonl while the dashboard sees a different feed.

Add a Postgres-backed sink that persists every Notification.Event, plus a read/query surface over MCP so any agent (and the operator) reads the same timeline. Mechanical facts only — the sink records and relays outcomes, never classifies or judges them (THE MANTRA). Persistence follows the repo rule: durable state is Ecto/Postgres under repo_enabled: true; repo_enabled: false degrades per store convention (ephemeral), never a new file store.

SUPERSEDED 2026-07-29 (roadmap review): folded into task 374 — its harness_events stream explicitly unifies the witness sink ("no second parallel event path"), so building this standalone Postgres sink first would be rework 374 immediately replaces. 374's ACs carry this task's deliverable (persisted witness timeline + MCP query) as part of the one stream.

task.title: Per-adapter/model activity trail across runs and agent seats
acceptance_criteria: Given an adapter and optional model, a bounded chronological query returns the persisted activity trail across implementer, reviewer, recovery, audit, and operator-triggered lifecycle seats, carrying run_id/project/seat/timestamp/outcome facts when present
New events use harness_events as the canonical read source after Task 374; ResultStore may supply clearly labelled historical compatibility rows only where pre-event history would otherwise disappear
A seat with no matching records is an empty list, never an error; pagination or a caller-supplied limit prevents an unbounded all-history read
Facts only: no computed score, ranking, route, or identity claim beyond relaying persisted adapter/model fields
Exposed as an Elixir API and api()-annotated MCP tool with JSON-expressible filters; tests cover multi-seat attribution, historical-source labelling when used, bounds, and the empty trail
out_of_scope: Stable human/member identity, keypairs, or identity continuity across adapter/model changes
Permission/capability enforcement
Extraction to a standalone library
Any change to routing, KPI computation, or reviewer selection
Nostr/Buzz integration
task.body:
Inspired by Block's Buzz audit trail, but deliberately narrower: harness has adapter/model
attribution, not a durable member identity. Build the query that the persisted facts support.
Given an adapter and optional model, return its bounded chronological activity across seats
and projects. Task 374's harness_events stream is the canonical source for newly recorded
seat facts; ResultStore is only a labelled compatibility source for history created before
that stream exists. Do not present an adapter/model pair as a stable person, member, or
cryptographic identity. The trail relays facts; routing and capability judgment stay with
the AIs reading them.

task.title: Unified append-only lifecycle event log (harness_events) — every run action becomes a durable, queryable fact
acceptance_criteria: A versioned append-only harness_events table/store records the closed lifecycle taxonomy after an explicit writer audit: dispatch enqueue, hold, steer, resume, cancel, resume_failed, rereview, reland, reviewer verdict, recovery outcome, land/blocked/conflict, post-merge audit, and approval park/approve; each event carries project, run_id when applicable, actor/seat, occurred_at, sequence/ordering metadata, schema version, and raw fact payload

Every writer supplies a stable idempotency key so Oban retries, repeated callbacks, and recovery re-entry cannot duplicate the same lifecycle fact; tests exercise duplicate append and ordering semantics

Append failure is surfaced at warn level or higher with event type/project/run id, never recursively writes another event, and does not silently claim a durable trace; existing run/landing outcome semantics remain unchanged
Park/approve decisions are recorded while PendingDispatch's documented soft-state contract remains unchanged

A bounded/index-backed cross-project Elixir + MCP query filters by project, event type, adapter/model actor, time range, and payload text, with pagination/limit and deterministic ordering. Payload text explicitly covers reviewer report and concerns prose on verdict events, so "which run raised this concern?" is one bounded query instead of per-run verdict_detail calls

Notification witness sinks consume or write through the same persisted event path; any deliberately separate delivery seam is documented as a projection of the stream, not a competing source of lifecycle truth
ResultStore remains the per-run aggregate/projection and harness_events the fine-grained lifecycle history; no migration pretends to reconstruct actor/seat facts that were never persisted

Facts only: no scoring, classification, or judgment arithmetic; repo_enabled: false degrades to the documented in-memory ephemeral store; tests cover every taxonomy member, multi-writer append, idempotency, append failure, park/approve trace, and bounded cross-project text query
out_of_scope: Cryptographic signing / per-agent keypairs (Buzz's Schnorr identity) — separate decision, only relevant beyond single-operator
Replacing ResultStore run records — they stay the per-run aggregate; the event log is the fine-grained stream beside them
Task 373's per-actor trail query surface — that task can consume this substrate but ships independently
Nostr/relay protocol compatibility
task.body: Inspired by Block's Buzz event history, but without importing its signed-identity claim: harness currently scatters lifecycle facts across ResultStore projections, Notification sinks, Oban rows, artifacts, and soft process state. Add one versioned append-only harness_events history beside ResultStore. The task is a repo-wide writer audit, not a suggestive sample: define a closed taxonomy, instrument every lifecycle mutation including operator recovery controls, and pin idempotency, ordering, append-failure, and query-bound contracts. Notification becomes a delivery projection of the same persisted facts; PendingDispatch stays intentionally soft state; ResultStore stays the per-run aggregate. Facts only — meaning remains with the agents that query them. Dispatch as a solo/exclusive wave because the write-set spans the lifecycle surface.

task.title: Validate optional %Harness.Project{} fields at registration — an uncast concurrency_cap silently kills batch dispatch
acceptance_criteria: Registering a project whose concurrency_cap is not a positive integer (string "4", 0, -1, a float) is rejected with an error result — the row is never persisted
The same validation holds for every registration entry point, not just the dashboard form: ProjectRegistry.upsert/1 and register/1 with an attrs map, and config-seeded entries

Every other optional field build_project/1 currently reads with a bare Map.get is validated to its @type: landing_policy, target_branch, reviewer, pollution_allowlist, warm_paths, test_db_isolation_env, tooling_baseline_overrides — or the moduledoc states why a given field is deliberately unvalidated
An already-persisted row that violates the type is reported at load time (Persistence.decode_rows already has a skip_invalid_row path) instead of being handed to callers
Tests cover the rejection of a string cap through upsert/1, and that a valid integer cap still round-trips through persist -> restart -> load
out_of_scope: Changing the dashboard forms — settings_live.ex already casts correctly via parse_concurrency_cap/1; the hole is the programmatic path behind it
Any change to how concurrency_cap is consumed (Oban.queue_limit/1, Batch.max_concurrency/2 stay as they are)
Migrating or rewriting existing rows beyond making an invalid one visible
task.body:
Found 2026-08-03 while auditing all 19 registrations against reality. Three projects — onchain_evm, onchain_js, onchain_tempo — carried `concurrency_cap: "4"` as a STRING. Consequence: `Harness.Batch.max_concurrency/2` guards on `is_integer(cap) and cap > 0`, but the string is truthy so it survives the `||` chain and lands in the guard, returning `{:error, {:invalid_max_concurrency, "4"}}` — batch dispatch was dead for those three projects. `Harness.Oban.queue_limit/1` separately fell through its own `is_integer` guard to the default limit, silently ignoring the operator's intent. Neither failure named the registration as the cause.

The dashboard cannot produce this: `settings_live.ex` casts via `parse_concurrency_cap/1`, which returns `:error` on anything non-integer. The value came in through the programmatic path — `ProjectRegistry.build_project/1` reads every optional field with a bare `Map.get(entry, :concurrency_cap)` and no cast or type check, while the required fields (name, source, roadmap_path, check_command, languages) all go through `fetch_*` validators. So the struct's `@type` is enforced on one half of its fields and merely documented on the other.

Fix the seam, not the one field: validate the whole optional set at build time so a registration that cannot work is rejected where it is created, not discovered as an unrelated error at dispatch time. The three bad rows were repaired by hand in Postgres on 2026-08-03; this task closes the hole that let them in.

task.title: Landing tests leak an empty temp repo dir per run into the shared worktree root
acceptance_criteria: Running the full suite twice leaves the same number of entries in the configured test worktree root as before the first run
No new `harness-repo-*` or `harness-suite-health-*` directory remains after the suite exits
Scratch repositories use a test-dedicated temporary root or a shared fixture with guaranteed on_exit cleanup; production worktree-root behavior is unchanged
Focused regression coverage proves cleanup on both successful and failing test paths without Process.sleep
out_of_scope: Stale harness/run-* branches and orphaned run worktrees — separate task
Changing the production worktree root location
task.body:
Running the suite leaves a `harness-repo-<pid>-<nanotime>/` directory behind in
the shared harness worktree root (`~/_DATA/worktrees/.harness/` on the dev host),
each containing only an empty `landing/` subdir. 2369 of them had accumulated as
of 2026-08-03, spanning 2026-06-13 to 2026-07-30 — i.e. every suite run since
mid-June has added more, and nothing has ever removed them.

They are empty, so this is not a disk problem; it is a signal problem. The
directory they pollute is the same root that holds real run worktrees, so
`ls` there no longer tells an operator anything, and any future sweep that walks
that root has to filter thousands of decoys first.

Find where the landing tests create that scratch root and make cleanup part of
the test lifecycle (ExUnit `tmp_dir` or an `on_exit` removal), so a suite run is
net-zero on the filesystem. Also decide whether test scratch belongs under the
*shared operator* worktree root at all — a dedicated tmp root would make the
leak self-evident instead of camouflaged.

**Update 2026-08-07 — backlog cleared by hand; the leak itself is untouched.**
The count had reached 2405 (plus ~60 `harness-suite-health-*` and one
`harness-warmtest`), newest stamped 2026-08-06 08:11 — so roughly 36 more
accumulated in the four days after this task was filed, confirming every suite
run still adds to it. All 2459 were removed manually during an unrelated
worktree-root cleanup, so the operator-visible symptom is gone and the root
now holds only real entries. That removes the pressure but not the defect: the
next suite run starts the pile over. Scope is therefore purely "stop the leak"
— do not treat the empty root as evidence of a fix or add a manual-cleanup deliverable.
Note the leak is not confined to `harness-repo-*`; the `harness-suite-health-*`
prefixes leak identically, so fix the shared scratch-root helper rather than
one test's cleanup.

task.title: Retry safe post-land cleanup and reclaim historical run branches/worktree orphans
acceptance_criteria: A regression test demonstrates the residual path by which the existing post-land prune can refuse cleanup while a run is still live, then proves a later bounded retry removes the landed branch/worktree once the commit is reachable from the target and the run is no longer live
Unlanded, failed, held, or otherwise sole-copy run branches/worktrees survive both automatic and maintenance passes

A dry-run maintenance entrypoint reports only landed branches whose commits are reachable from the configured target; its apply mode can reclaim the historical branch backlog without touching retained work
Unregistered orphan directories and worktrees whose .git back-link names a moved/renamed main checkout are detected; the report distinguishes git-native repair from safe removal
Existing successful-land cleanup and boot-sweeper behavior remain covered; cleanup/refusal errors are surfaced rather than silently discarded
out_of_scope: Test-suite temp directory leakage — separate task
Rewriting the lander's ff-push path
task.body:
The original task premise was wrong: successful landing cleanup already exists.
`Harness.Lander` calls `prune_landed_run/3`, which delegates to
`Worktree.cleanup_for_run/2`; `lander_test.exs` proves successful lands remove the
branch/worktree, and `Harness.Worktree.Sweeper` performs a boot sweep. Task 275 and
commit 469216b introduced that behavior.

The residual defect is that cleanup may be refused while the run is still considered live,
with no later retry after liveness clears. Historical branches therefore accumulate even
though the happy path is implemented. Diagnose and close that timing/retry gap, then provide
a conservative maintenance path for the backlog: delete only when the run's commits are
provably reachable from the configured target; retain the sole copy of failed/unlanded work.

Two filesystem orphan classes also need observable handling. Some directories outlive git
registration, so `git worktree list/prune` cannot see them. Others keep a `.git` file whose
back-link names a moved or renamed main checkout; prune reports nothing and remove refuses
the worktree. Inspect the back-link and report whether `git worktree repair` can preserve the
run or whether landed/reachable data is safe to remove. The directory backlog was cleared by
hand on 2026-08-07; the retained branch backlog and missing later-retry policy remain.

task.title: Durable roadmap writes ignore roadmap_path and push tasks.toml into the source repo
acceptance_criteria: For a project whose roadmap_path and source resolve to two different git repositories, a mark_* transition commits and pushes the roadmap change in the ROADMAP repository; the source repository's branches, worktrees and working tree are untouched by it
For that same project, code delivery is unaffected: the run worktree still forks from source and the lander still ff-pushes the delivery commit to source's target_branch
When roadmap_path and source resolve to the same repository, behavior is unchanged — the existing durability tests pass without being edited
The branch the roadmap commit is pushed to is explicit rather than inferred from the code target: either a validated project field or a stated derivation, documented on %Harness.Project{}

A roadmap repository with no resolvable push target, and a roadmap_path outside any git repository, both fall back to the plain local rmap write and return an error or a documented degraded result rather than pushing to a guessed branch or raising
The local-checkout fast-forward that follows a durable write targets the roadmap repository, not the source repository
A test using two separate temporary repositories proves the roadmap commit is reachable in the roadmap repo and absent from the source repo after a mark_landed transition
%Harness.Project{}'s docs state, per field, which repository it governs — enough that an operator registering a split project cannot guess wrong
out_of_scope: The rmap-side per-task target repo (rmap task 54). That field says where WORK lands; this task is only about where the roadmap WRITE goes. Renderable is not executable — do not build consumption of an rmap field that does not exist yet
Where the implementer worktree forks from. Code work continues to fork off source; nothing about dispatch or delivery changes
The read path. ingest/list/next_bundle already resolve through roadmap_path and are correct
landing_policy semantics, the lander's conflict/retry behavior, and the audit worker
task.body:
`%Harness.Project{}` carries `source` (where the repository lives) and
`roadmap_path` (the directory holding `roadmap/tasks.toml`) as two independent
enforced keys, and the read path honors that separation — `resolve_root/1`
expands `project.roadmap_path`, so ingest, list and next_bundle all read the
right file. The **durable write path does not**, and it is the write that has
side effects.

`Harness.Roadmap.apply_mutation/6` is the chokepoint every `mark_*` transition
funnels through. It asks `durable_target/1` where to write, and that function
resolves the repository from `Project.local_repo_path/1` — i.e. from **`source`**
— pairing it with `target_branch`. `Durable.commit/3` then forks a detached
worktree at that repo's freshly-fetched `origin/<target>`, runs the rmap
mutation against `<worktree>/roadmap/tasks.toml`, commits `roadmap: task N ->
done`, ff-pushes it, and finally fast-forwards the operator's local checkout of
that same repo via `Harness.Git.TargetSync`. `roadmap_path` appears nowhere in
that sequence; it is consulted only by `landing_root/1`, which serves the
`:none` fallback — the branch taken when a project has no `target_branch` or no
operable local checkout.

Every federated project has a `target_branch`, so in practice the durable path
always wins and `roadmap_path` is silently dead for writes. That is invisible
while both fields point at one repository, which is true of all 19 registrations
today. It stops being invisible the moment they diverge: harness would fork a
worktree of the code repository, look for `roadmap/tasks.toml` where there is
none, and — depending on how the rmap shell-out fails — either error out on
every landing or push a roadmap commit into a repository that has no roadmap.

The concrete case that surfaced it: `bourse` was split on 2026-08-04 into a
public client repository that is published to hex, and a private workbench that
keeps the 500+ task roadmap, the scoring, the assignees and the consumer bug
queue. The intended registration is `roadmap_path` = workbench, `source` =
client. The registered project still points both at the workbench, because
pointing `source` at the client would fork worktrees where the roadmap does not
exist. So the split is currently un-dispatchable, and the field that was
supposed to express it does not carry.

Make the durable write go where the roadmap actually is. The read path already
shows the intended shape; this is making the write agree with it. Note that the
roadmap repository needs its own push target — `target_branch` names the branch
*code* lands on, and there is no reason a separate roadmap repository shares its
name. Decide how that is expressed and make the failure mode conservative: when
harness cannot determine a roadmap push target with certainty, it must fall back
to the local write it already has rather than push a roadmap commit to a branch
it guessed.
task.implemented: Landed by codex via merge-train; reviewer-approved (run run-1785889900340-3393925d, b4d525e8beeaf3b3557bea84c0d586ac773d60b3).

task.title: Durable roadmap writeback silently produced no commit — dispatch-start and post-land transitions both lost
acceptance_criteria: A durable roadmap write that does not land its commit on the target branch surfaces at warn level or higher, naming the transition, task id, run id, and the concrete Durable error reason — a silent no-op is no longer a reachable outcome.

An integration test drives both transitions (dispatch-start in_progress, post-land done) against a fixture project whose operator checkout is dirty AND ahead of origin, and asserts the target branch receives a roadmap commit for each.

After a successful land in that test, the target branch's tasks.toml shows the task done carrying verified, verified_by, verification_ref and shipped_in, and started_at set by the earlier dispatch-start transition.
The root cause of the two lost transitions in run-1785889534260-fc424f54 is named explicitly in the implemented field — not just patched around.
Behavior on a clean, in-sync operator checkout is unchanged, and no force-push is introduced on any path.
out_of_scope: Changing rmap's validate-then-write contract or its implemented-required-on-done invariant (that is the rmap repo's surface)
Committing or stashing the operator's unrelated dirty working-tree files
Reworking the landing train, the reviewer gate, or the run lifecycle beyond the writeback call sites
task.body:
A full green run wrote nothing back to the roadmap, and nothing said so.

Evidence — run `run-1785889534260-fc424f54`, project `rmap`, task 53. The run was
approved by the reviewer gate and landed on the target branch (`origin/main`, sha
`8f88d25`, two harness delivery commits). But NEITHER roadmap transition took
effect: task 53 never went `in_progress` (no `started_at` was ever written) and
never went `done` after landing (no `shipped_in`, no `verified`). It read `pending`
both in the operator checkout and in `origin/main`'s own `roadmap/tasks.toml`, and
`origin/main` carries no `roadmap:` commit for the run at all. The operator had to
write the outcome by hand.

`Harness.Roadmap.Durable` is supposed to make this impossible: mutate in a throwaway
detached worktree at the freshly-fetched origin tip, commit, ff-push, then ff-sync
the operator's local target. The push half is what failed — there is no commit on
origin to sync from.

Two candidate causes are already ruled out, do not re-derive them:

  * It is NOT rmap's `implemented`-required-on-`done` gate. `Harness.Lander` does
    pass `implemented:` into `Roadmap.mark_landed/2` (lib/harness/lander.ex:719),
    and `--implemented` is appended when supplied (lib/harness/roadmap.ex:362).
    That gate would also not explain the missing `in_progress` transition, which
    has no such requirement.
  * The step-5 local ff-sync skip is NOT sufficient. `Durable`'s moduledoc
    documents that `Harness.Git.TargetSync` deliberately leaves a dirty or diverged
    operator checkout alone — and the checkout WAS both dirty and one unpushed
    commit ahead at the time. But that only explains a stale local copy; it does
    not explain the absent commit on origin.

Find out what actually happened to those two transitions, fix it, and — the part
that matters as much as the fix — make this failure mode loud. A durable write that
cannot land its commit must not look identical to one that succeeded. Today the
writeback is best-effort by design (a failed transition logs and never fails the
run, which is the right call), but "never fails the run" has become "never reaches
the operator either".

Second instance, 2026-08-12 — run `run-1786522856472-c6cebe49`, project
`trading_dashboard`, task 59. Narrower shape than the first: the in_progress
transition DID land, and the delivery itself landed on origin/main (5309118 +
reviewer-fix 924e059; ResultStore record carries landed_sha=924e0594b5e4), but the
post-land done transition never produced a roadmap commit AND the lander's own
"harness lander: landed task 59" info line is absent from the node log — while the
very next landing on the same serialized queue (task 53, run
run-1786522854280-f22c65ba, ~minutes later) completed fully, writeback and log line
included. So whatever fails is per-landing, not environmental, and it can kill both
the mark_landed writeback and the success log of one landing while its neighbor
succeeds — consistent with the landing job dying between ff-push and writeback.
Operator repaired by hand (trading_dashboard commit 7319255).

task.title: Fetch each project target once per landed-sha reconciliation pass
acceptance_criteria: One dashboard reconciliation pass fetches each project's target ref at most once regardless of the number of unlanded history rows
Rows for different projects resolve against their own fetched target and preserve existing landed-sha semantics
Fetch failures remain observable and do not reuse another project's ref
Focused tests count fetches for multiple rows/projects; mix check.dispatch is green
out_of_scope: Changing the 30-second roadmap tick
KPI aggregate bounding, transcript buffering, or ProjectRegistry caching
task.body: The dashboard reconciles unlanded run-history rows on mount and each roadmap tick. The current path calls ResultStore.reconcile_landed_sha/4 per row, which reaches fetch_target/2 and performs a real git fetch each time. Change the reconciliation pass so target-ref retrieval is shared only within one project/pass, while row-level landed-sha decisions and failure visibility remain unchanged. This is the former H2 part of Task 358, split because it has a separate git/dashboard seam and verification surface.

task.title: Make capped dashboard transcript append linear in incoming chunk size
acceptance_criteria: Appending a port chunk no longer copies the complete retained transcript buffer on every call
The existing 200 KiB cap, parsing output, event ordering, and connected-viewer behavior are unchanged
Focused tests cover incremental append, cap truncation, and chunk boundaries without relying on timing
mix check.dispatch is green
out_of_scope: Changing transcript parsing or presentation
Changing the retained-byte cap
Other dashboard query work
task.body: Harness.Dashboard.Transcript.append/3 currently evaluates buffer <> chunk for each port chunk, copying the retained buffer repeatedly up to the 200 KiB cap for every connected viewer. Preserve the public behavior and cap while making incremental accumulation linear in the new chunk size, materializing only at the existing parse/render boundary. This is the former M2 part of Task 358, split because it is an isolated data-structure change.

task.title: Remove the per-lookup Postgres landing-settings round trip from ProjectRegistry
acceptance_criteria: ProjectRegistry.lookup/1 does not query Postgres for landing overrides on every call
Writes to landing/project settings invalidate or refresh the read path so lookup and list return the same current project view
repo_enabled: false preserves the documented in-memory behavior
Focused tests count persistence reads across repeated lookup and verify update visibility; mix check.dispatch is green
out_of_scope: Changing project registration semantics
Caching unrelated stores
Other dashboard performance work
task.body: ProjectRegistry.lookup/1 overlays landing settings with a fresh single-project Postgres read on each call, including dashboard task-detail hot paths, while list/0 already batches the overlay. Give lookup the same bounded read behavior or keep the rarely-changing overrides in registry state with explicit invalidation on writes. Preserve the persisted source of truth and current lookup/list results. This is the former M3 part of Task 358, split because it changes registry/cache coherence rather than dashboard rendering.

task.title: Delivery commit exclusion missed .harness/agent-rules.md — harness's own scaffolding rode in a deliverable
acceptance_criteria: A run whose worktree contains .harness/agent-rules.md (and any other .harness/ file) produces a delivery commit with zero .harness/ paths — pinned by a test at the staging/commit layer
The root cause is named in the fix (which staging step missed the file and why)
task.body:
Observed on bourse run run-1786333517477-27a62f4d (task 552, delivery commit 5acb63c, 2026-08-10): the delivery commit contains .harness/agent-rules.md — harness's own dispatch-time prompt file ("You are being driven by harness…"). The workflow contract says .harness/ is excluded from delivery commits so runtime scaffolding never rides in a deliverable; the exclusion evidently misses this file (or the file is written at a moment the staging exclusion does not cover). The consumer repo had no .gitignore entry for .harness/, so the file landed tracked on main and was removed by the orchestrator (bourse commit 1b84d7f, which also added .harness/ to that repo's .gitignore — a consumer-side mitigation, not the fix).

Find where the delivery staging computes its exclusion set and why agent-rules.md escaped it; pin the fix with a test that stages a run worktree containing .harness/agent-rules.md and asserts the delivery commit is free of any .harness/ path.

task.title: Migrate anubis_mcp 1.x -> 2.0.0 (Application callback removal, transport/supervision rewrite)
acceptance_criteria: mix.exs constraint for anubis_mcp raised to allow 2.0.0 and mix.lock resolves it

Harness.Application explicitly starts/supervises whatever anubis_mcp 2.0.0 requires now that its own Application callback + bundled CLI are removed (harness already declares its own child spec today, per Task 79/83 — confirm the new API keeps the same explicit-start shape or adapt it)
The Streamable HTTP transport at /harness/mcp keeps working end to end (initialize, tools/list, tools/call) against a real claude -p client, per the Task 83 smoke-test pattern
Resource blob encoding change (v2.0.0 standardizes to base64) does not break any harness MCP tool response consumed by the dashboard or a headless client

mix check.dispatch is green and existing MCP server tests (test/harness/dashboard/mcp_server_test.exs and related) pass unmodified in behavior, or are updated to match the new API with equivalent coverage
out_of_scope: Re-adding HTTP+SSE transport support (removed upstream, harness already uses Streamable HTTP only)
Any change to which MCP tools harness exposes (Harness.Chat.Tools stays the source of truth)
The anubis_mcp LGPL licensing decision (tracked separately, Task with title 'Decision: resolve the anubis_mcp LGPL-3.0 ...')
task.body:
2026-08-13 hex-lib upgrade pass: mix.exs pins {:anubis_mcp, "~> 1.6"} (currently locked at 1.14.0); hex.pm's latest is 2.0.0, blocked purely by that constraint (mix hex.outdated confirms: no transitive pin involved). anubis_mcp's own changelog (https://anubis-mcp.hexdocs.pm/changelog.html) documents real breaking changes for 2.0.0: removal of the HTTP+SSE client/server transports (harness already uses Streamable HTTP, so likely unaffected), a raised minimum MCP protocol version floor (2024-11-05 -> 2025-03-26), removal of the Application callback + bundled CLI (carried forward from 1.8.0 - "applications no longer automatically start supervision trees... developers must explicitly start relevant components in their own supervision tree"), and standardized base64 resource blob encoding.

harness's Harness.Dashboard.MCPServer (Task 79/83) already supervises its own child spec explicitly (Harness.Application starts {Harness.Dashboard.MCPServer, transport: {:streamable_http, start: true}}), so the Application-callback removal may be a non-event here -- but this needs verifying against the 2.0.0 API surface, not assumed. Left un-upgraded in the 2026-08-13 bulk dependency bump specifically because it is a breaking major touching harness's own MCP driver surface (the surface skills/harness-driver/SKILL.md and CLAUDE.md's "MCP (Harness.Dashboard.MCPServer, on anubis_mcp)" describe as load-bearing), not a mechanical hex.lock bump -- it deserves its own reviewed diff and a live claude -p smoke test, per the Task 83 precedent (a supervision/transport-start mismatch there caused a silent :badarg on every MCP request).
task.implemented: Bumped mix.exs anubis_mcp ~> 1.6 -> ~> 2.0; mix deps.update resolved 2.0.0 cleanly, zero transitive conflicts. Compiled clean, 20/20 MCP tests pass unmodified, mix check.dispatch green (doctor 100%, sobelow clean) -- no lib/ or test/ changes needed. Live verification: user restarted the harness BEAM node; ran a full session over the real /harness/mcp Streamable HTTP endpoint on 2.0.0 -- initialize (negotiated protocolVersion 2025-11-25, mcp-session-id issued) -> notifications/initialized (202) -> tools/list (full catalog returned) -> tools/call agents-list (real result payload). Driven via curl with clientInfo spoofed as claude-code/2.1.153, not the actual claude -p binary -- close to but not identical to the AC's literal 'real claude -p client' wording; the wire-level MCP session lifecycle is nonetheless fully exercised end to end against the live server. Shipped in 7655dda + 2bc1623.

task.title: Strip the harness-injected ephemeral AGENTS.md header before committing the delivery
acceptance_criteria: A run whose worktree carries the injected '<!-- harness-injected: canonical agent rules — ephemeral, do not commit -->' AGENTS.md block never includes that block in the delivery commit: the injected content is reverted/excluded at the commit step regardless of whether the implementer or reviewer touched AGENTS.md otherwise

A test pins the invariant: given a worktree where AGENTS.md differs from the base only by the injected header, the delivery commit leaves AGENTS.md byte-identical to the base; given a worktree where AGENTS.md has both the header and a legitimate regen, the commit carries the regen but not the header
Existing exclusion list behavior (.harness/, roadmap files, CHANGELOG) is unchanged
A target repo that tracks its own AGENTS.md has that file byte-identical before and after a run whose agent did not intentionally edit it

Coverage is per-adapter, not per-instance: a regression test reproduces the leak against the adapter that produced the second occurrence (cursor) before the fix, and every adapter's injection path is covered
The reason Task 36's criterion did not hold for this path is named explicitly in the implemented field, rather than the leak simply being re-patched
out_of_scope: Changing what the injected block says or when it is injected
AGENTS.md freshness checking (sync-agents-md --check remains the consumer-side gate)
task.body:
Harness prepends an ephemeral agent-rules block to the target project's AGENTS.md when dispatching ('harness-injected: canonical agent rules — ephemeral, do not commit'). That block leaked into a landed delivery commit: trading_dashboard run run-1786673501096-c9939b07 (task 68) landed commit 2132b41 whose AGENTS.md diff is exactly the 32-line injected header — despite the reviewer explicitly noting AGENTS.md was 'excluded from this delivery'. The parallel run for task 58 saw the same stale-AGENTS.md red in mix check.dispatch; the orchestrator had to strip the header manually on the landed base (trading_dashboard commit 'AGENTS.md regen: strip harness-injected ephemeral header leaked by task 68 delivery').

The commit step must guarantee the injected content never rides in a delivery: restore/revert the injected block before git add (the same way .harness/ and roadmap files are excluded), so downstream sync-agents-md --check and cross-family reviewers do not chase phantom AGENTS.md drift. Evidence: trading_dashboard commits 2132b41 (leak) and the follow-up regen commit; reviewer reports of runs run-1786673501096-c9939b07 and run-1786673495073-4130d146 both document the mechanism.

SECOND OCCURRENCE, different repo and adapter (folded in from the duplicate Task 390, 2026-08-21): onchain_aave commit cfb58b1 — agent delivery for its task 50, run run-1787296526753-07002de8, adapter cursor — added the same 32-line block to that repo's tracked AGENTS.md and reached origin/main. It surfaced only afterwards, when the consuming repo's own mix ci failed its AGENTS.md-freshness gate; a repo without such a gate would never notice. Task 36 closed with the criterion "Existing AGENTS.md in the target repo (if any) is not modified by the harness-injected block ending up in the run's delivery commit" — that criterion is violated again, so the fix must explain why the earlier one did not cover this path.

Worth checking during diagnosis, as a hypothesis and not a confirmed root cause: Harness.AgentAdapter documents the AGENTS.md channel as Codex's (@codex_agents_rel), while the observed leak came from a cursor run — so either the per-adapter channel mapping does not hold at runtime, or the cross-family reviewer (codex) wrote into the worktree before the delivery commit was taken. Confirm before building on it.

task.title: Lander: landing job can complete (landed_sha recorded) without the roadmap advance ever reaching origin
acceptance_criteria: A landing whose rmap-advance commit or push fails does not settle the Oban job as completed: it retries or errors loudly, and never records landed_sha while origin lacks the advance
A regression test covers the delivery-pushed-but-advance-failed path
dispatch-reland on a run with a recorded landed_sha and no surviving branch performs an advance-only reland instead of discarding with checkout_failed (test)
out_of_scope: Changing the witness sink or notification format
task.body:
Observed trading_dashboard 2026-08-14: task 64's landing job (Oban job 6898, queue landing_trading_dashboard) finished state=completed at 05:02:16Z, the ResultStore record carries landed_sha 92d18a91f0d4 (delivery 36537ec + two reviewer commits, all on origin/main), the run branch was cleaned up — but NO "roadmap: task 64 -> done" commit ever reached origin. The next landing on the same queue (task 56, job 6900, 25s later) pushed delivery AND advance normally. Consequence: origin diverged from the lander's own record — rmap still said in_progress for landed work, which is exactly the duplicate-land trap the workflow include warns about, except this time the STALE side was origin itself, so no amount of fetch/rebase could disprove "didn't land". The orchestrator had to hand-write the advance (trading_dashboard 9b6f4ab) with provenance copied from the ResultStore.

Two asks:
1. Find and fix the path where Lander.Worker returns :ok after pushing the delivery but before (or despite) the rmap-advance commit/push failing — the advance must be part of the landing's success criterion, or the job must retry/fail loudly instead of completing.
2. Make dispatch-reland usable for this state: job 6902 (manual_reland) discarded with {:checkout_failed, {:git_failed, ... "invalid reference: harness/run-1786680419733-0929c71f"}} because the branch was already deleted by the successful code landing. When the persisted record has a landed_sha and the branch is gone, reland should degrade to advance-only (re-run the rmap advance + push) instead of discarding on worktree checkout.

Premise verified: Oban job rows 6898/6900/6902 and the ResultStore record were read live on 2026-08-14; trading_dashboard origin/main history 36537ec..9b6f4ab shows the gap.

Second occurrence, same day: trading_dashboard task 101 (run run-1786691814297-f2b6f148, grok/codex) — landing job completed, landed_sha ce880b3 recorded, delivery + review commits and even the post-merge audit landed on origin, but the "task 101 -> done" advance was again never pushed and was hand-written by the orchestrator (trading_dashboard 717addf). The bug is reproducible, not a one-off.

task.title: Build a fleet task Kanban from rmap and Harness lifecycle facts
acceptance_criteria: The existing /harness/roadmap route presents Pending, Implementing, Reviewing, Landing, Blocked, and Done lanes across registered projects, with a project filter and a bounded recent-Done result set

Pending, Blocked, and Done placement comes from rmap; Pending cards expose dependency readiness, while Implementing, Reviewing, and Landing placement comes from persisted or live Harness lifecycle facts
Each card shows the available project, task id, title, assignee/model, active run stage, elapsed-time, and cost/token facts without fabricating missing values

Eligible cards expose only existing dispatch, hold/resume, review-recovery, and landing actions; the board refreshes after success and presents the existing operation error without silently changing task state
A failed or held run is relayed as a factual badge and action state; code does not compute urgency, health, stuckness, or priority from those facts
No new rmap status, lifecycle store, or duplicate task projection becomes authoritative
LiveView tests cover every lane, dependency-ready and dependency-waiting Pending cards, project filtering, bounded Done history, successful and rejected actions, empty states, and multiple projects
Operator-facing route or dashboard documentation that enumerates the roadmap surface remains accurate
out_of_scope: Drag-and-drop or free-form lane movement
Creating or editing rmap tasks from the dashboard
New lifecycle event types or persistence
Cost, runner, files, or knowledge-management dashboards
task.body: Turn the existing read-only RoadmapLive surface into a project-spanning task board. rmap remains authoritative for durable task status, while Harness run, result, and lifecycle-event facts provide execution and landing context. Present the workflow as factual lanes with direct actions that reuse existing dispatch and recovery contracts; do not add drag-and-drop or a second task-state model.

task.title: Add an operator Action Inbox and durable Activity view
acceptance_criteria: Separate /harness/inbox and /harness/activity routes appear in dashboard navigation; Inbox displays the current count of unresolved supported actions

Inbox includes parked manual dispatch approvals, held runs, failed committed runs eligible for resume or rereview, and approved runs eligible for land or reland, using existing eligibility facts and guards

Approve, Resume, Resume Failed, Rereview, Land, and Reland invoke the existing Harness operation contracts directly; success updates or removes the row without a full reload, and errors remain visible without being treated as success

Activity presents deterministic, paginated lifecycle history with bounded filters for project, run, event type, adapter/model, time range, and payload text using the Task 374 and Task 373 query surfaces
Activity clearly labels any historical compatibility rows supplied by ResultStore and shows an empty result as an empty list rather than an error
When repository persistence is disabled, the views identify the event history as ephemeral without claiming durability
The UI relays facts and available operations only; it does not compute severity, urgency, stuckness, health, ranking, or routing judgments
LiveView and supporting context tests cover every direct action and guard failure, live count updates, filters, pagination, deterministic ordering, ephemeral mode, empty states, and operation errors
Operator-facing documentation that enumerates dashboard routes and controls remains accurate
out_of_scope: Creating, editing, reprioritizing, or dragging rmap tasks
A new event store, event taxonomy, or notification channel
Acknowledgement state for informational warnings
Automated action prioritization, severity scoring, or lifecycle diagnosis
Cost, runner, files, or knowledge-management dashboards
task.body: Add separate operator Inbox and Activity dashboard surfaces over the lifecycle contracts delivered by Tasks 374 and 373. The Inbox is an explicit queue of interventions supported by existing Harness operations; Activity is a bounded chronological view of persisted lifecycle facts. Reuse the Dispatch facade and event-query APIs rather than reimplementing action eligibility, storage, or meaning in LiveView code.

task.title: Expose roadmap_target_branch on the operator registration surfaces
acceptance_criteria: dispatch-register_project accepts an optional roadmap_target_branch scalar and persists it on the registered %Harness.Project{}
The /harness/settings project create/edit form reads and writes roadmap_target_branch (blank stays nil)
priv/repo/seeds.exs.example documents the field next to target_branch, including that it is required when roadmap_path and source are different repositories
skills/harness-driver/SKILL.md names the field on dispatch-register_project and on the Project struct
An invalid branch name is rejected at registration with {:invalid_roadmap_target_branch, _} — same rule ProjectRegistry already applies on the programmatic path
Existing same-repo registrations that omit the field still derive the durable branch from target_branch
out_of_scope: Changing durable-write resolution itself (Task 378 already shipped that)
Task 375's broader optional-field validation sweep — this task only wires the new field onto the operator surfaces; 375 still owns the rest of the optional set
Changing lander/code-delivery target_branch semantics
task.body:
Task 378 added `%Harness.Project{roadmap_target_branch}` so durable `mark_*`
writes can target a roadmap repository that is not the code `source`. The
field is load-bearing for any split-repo registration (the bourse
public-client / private-workbench case that motivated 378): without an
explicit branch, a split project falls back to a local rmap write and the
roadmap never advances on origin.

Evidence (read 2026-08-16, this audit of 31cfd94):
- `Harness.Dispatch.register_project/8` has no `roadmap_target_branch` param
  (`lib/harness/dispatch.ex`).
- `/harness/settings` create/edit form has no mention of the field
  (`lib/harness/dashboard/` grep is empty).
- `priv/repo/seeds.exs.example` only documents `target_branch`.

So the only way to set the field today is a keyword/struct
`ProjectRegistry.upsert/1` from IEx. An operator following the dashboard or
MCP registration path cannot express the split 378 was built to support.

Do not fold this into Task 375. 375 is a validation sweep of the *pre-378*
optional set and explicitly leaves dashboard forms out of scope. This task
is the missing authoring surface for one new field.

The seeds example in this audit already carries a one-line comment pointing
at the field; keep or expand that rather than treating the comment as the
deliverable.

task.title: Four `roadmap-mark_*` MCP tools expose zero parameters — declare their params, then guard the class
acceptance_criteria: `roadmap-mark_landed`, `roadmap-mark_blocked`, `roadmap-mark_in_progress` and `roadmap-mark_pending` each expose their documented arguments in the MCP tool schema, and each is callable end to end over MCP against a registered project

A test asserts the invariant for the whole module, not the four instances: every `@descripex_api_declarations` entry in `Harness.Roadmap` whose backing function has arity > 0 declares a non-empty parameter set
The moduledoc'd option lists and the declared parameter sets agree — a documented option that is not declared fails the new test
out_of_scope: Changing what the mark_* functions do, or their Elixir arities — the lander calls them directly and is unaffected
Auditing api/2 declarations in modules other than `Harness.Roadmap`
task.body:
`Harness.Roadmap` declares seven MCP tools. Three (`ingest`, `ready`, `list`) use descripex's `api/3` and pass a parameter list. The four `mark_*` tools use `api/2`, which accumulates the declaration with `opts = []` — so the generated MCP schema is `{"properties": {}, "required": []}` even though each function's moduledoc documents `:project` / `:root` / `:reason` / `:rmap_bin`, and each Elixir function is `arity 2` and `Keyword.fetch!`es a required option.

Observed from onchain_evm on 2026-08-22: calling `mcp__harness__roadmap-mark_blocked` fails with `Harness.Roadmap.mark_blocked/0 is undefined or private`. The tool is advertised, documented, and unusable. The other three are declared identically and so are broken the same way; only `mark_blocked` has been exercised.

Blast radius is bounded — `Harness.Lander.Resilience` calls `Roadmap.mark_blocked/2` in-process, so autonomous landing is unaffected. What is broken is the orchestrator's ability to park or re-route a task over MCP, which is exactly the seat that needs it when a wave goes sideways.

Fix the four declarations, and then close the class rather than the four instances: the failure mode is that an `api/2` declaration on a function that takes arguments compiles cleanly, documents itself correctly, and only fails at call time from a client. A module-level test over the declaration accumulator turns that into a compile-or-test failure.

task.title: Terminate the agent process tree, not just the direct PID — orphaned children outlive the kill and share the worktree
acceptance_criteria: Every termination path kills the whole descendant process tree of the agent, not only the immediate OS pid: the AgentAdapter terminate/1 default, OSProcess.kill/1, reviewer timeout and rotation, dispatch-cancel, hold with interrupt, and idle/lifetime/total timeout expiry

Termination escalates rather than going straight to SIGKILL: tree SIGTERM, then a bounded grace window, then tree SIGKILL. The grace window is an operator-visible configuration fact with a documented default; agent CLIs flush their transcript tail on SIGTERM, so the ordering is load-bearing

A caller that tears down or REUSES a worktree waits for tree quiescence first: after a kill returns, no descendant of the agent pid is still alive before the worktree is torn down or a replacement reviewer is spawned into it

Harness.Run.MemoryGuard.kill_tree/1 stops being the sole owner of tree-kill: the implementation lives on the shared process-lifecycle surface and MemoryGuard consumes it, so a future termination path cannot silently regress to single-pid kill

Tests spawn an agent stand-in that forks a long-lived grandchild and assert, per termination path, that the grandchild is gone; that SIGTERM precedes SIGKILL; and that quiescence holds before worktree teardown and before a rotation reviewer is spawned
OSProcess's moduledoc no longer documents orphaning as accepted behavior with the boot-time Worktree.Sweeper as the backstop
out_of_scope: Adding termination fields to Outcome or Result — kind (:exited / {:timed_out, :idle|:total} / {:reflex_halted,_} / {:error,_}) and the advisory exit_status already carry these facts orthogonally
Parsing agent output to infer that a run is stuck
Changing timeout durations or the watchdog policy
Windows process-tree support
Removing the boot-time Worktree.Sweeper — it stays as a backstop for crashed nodes
task.body:
Harness.AgentAdapter.OSProcess.kill/1 SIGKILLs only the immediate OS pid; its own moduledoc states the consequence: "tool subprocesses the agent itself spawned can be orphaned by that." An agent CLI is never a leaf — it spawns mix test, dialyzer, rg, node. Harness.Run.MemoryGuard.kill_tree/1 already implements the correct behavior (ps table -> descendants -> kill each) but is wired only to the memory watchdog via Run.Actions.Control; every other termination path leaks the tree.

The sharpest instance is reviewer rotation. In lib/harness/run/actions/reviewing.ex, a reviewer idle-timeout calls terminate_reviewer/1 — single-pid kill — and then :repeat_state spawns the NEXT reviewer into the SAME worktree. Reviewer A's orphaned `mix test` keeps running against the tree that reviewer B is now checking: concurrent writes to _build, a shared test database, and lock files, from a process harness believes it killed. That is a false-red/false-green generator in exactly the bug class the agent-gate rebuild set out to end, and it is pure substrate — no judgment involved.

Idea confirmed against DeepSeek Harness (packages/subprocess: terminate() is tree-scoped on every platform, escalates SIGTERM -> grace -> SIGKILL, is idempotent, and is paired with a waitForExit that observes whole-tree liveness) and its docs/defensive-patterns.md rule "Dispose must reach quiescence, not just request it": a teardown that issues kills and returns before the work stops leaves orphans.

task.title: Fence .harness/review.json to the reviewer that wrote it — a killed reviewer's stale approve can settle the run :done
acceptance_criteria: The verdict artifact is removed before EVERY reviewer spawn — primary, re-prompt, rotation, and dispatch-rereview — so a read after a spawn can never return an earlier reviewer's file

Each reviewer invocation carries run identity and review-attempt number in its Port environment; the reviewer prompt requires echoing both into the artifact, and a mismatch is treated as {:error, :missing}, routing into the existing re-prompt/rotation ladder instead of settling the run

The implementer transcript handed to the reviewer states when it is a tail: the elided byte count and the total, so the reviewer knows it is not seeing the whole run. The 40 KB @reviewer_transcript_tail_bytes slice is currently unlabelled, and the recovery prompt's transcript_tail has the same gap

Tests pin the false-approve path: reviewer A writes verdict approve and is then killed, reviewer B is rotated in and writes nothing — the run must NOT settle :done on A's artifact. Separate tests cover attempt-identity mismatch routing to re-prompt, and the truncation marker appearing only when the transcript actually exceeded the tail size
out_of_scope: Changing task_outcomes gating — reviewing.ex already fails closed: a malformed block parses to %{} and Enum.all?(ids, &(Map.get(...) == "approved")) then rejects with an explicit reason, so there is no false-green there
Changing free-form block parsing — facets/skills/ratings/checks/concerns stay fail-open by design (open vocabulary, persisted verbatim)
Adding a schema version to the artifact — speculative while the one gating field is already fail-closed
Changing the tail size, or the dashboard's 200 KiB buffer cap (Task 381 owns that buffer; the Driver's own accumulation is unbounded and complete)
Reworking reviewer rotation or the re-prompt limit themselves
task.body:
Harness.Run.Review.read/1 (lib/harness/run/review.ex:117) is a bare Artifact.read of .harness/review.json plus a JSON decode. Nothing removes the file before a reviewer spawns, and nothing binds it to the reviewer instance that wrote it. Three live paths reuse the same worktree and can therefore hand harness a verdict from a reviewer that is no longer the one being waited on: rotation on reviewer timeout, the capped re-prompt (@reviewer_reprompt_limit 1), and dispatch-rereview against a retained branch.

The concrete false-green: reviewer A writes {"verdict": "approve"}, then hangs mid-check and is idle-killed; rotation spawns reviewer B into the same worktree; B crashes or writes nothing; harness reads A's file and settles :done. The run lands on an approve from a reviewer that never finished checking. Both fixes are pure mechanics — deleting a file before a spawn, and comparing two strings — and the mismatch case routes into recovery machinery that already exists.

Folded in from the same surface (reviewing.ex, reviewer-spawn path): the transcript handed to the reviewer is a deliberate 40 KB tail via transcript_tail/1, but it is presented without any marker saying so. The reviewer cannot tell a short complete transcript from the last 40 KB of a long one, and neither can the recovery AI, which is given "minimal context" it has no way to know is incomplete. Counting the elided bytes and stating the number is mechanics.

Idea confirmed against DeepSeek Harness packages/feedback: every stored row carries the inspected session's header identity and "a mismatch is treated as absence", which fences a reused session id whose identity differs.

task.title: Gate runner: declare check dependencies, run independent gates in parallel, capture one log per gate
acceptance_criteria: A gate is declared with an id, a label, the command to run, its dependencies, and an optional allow-failure flag; the check aggregates (check.fast, check.dispatch, precommit, precommit.full/ci) are expressed as gate sets over that declaration instead of serial alias lists

Independent gates within one aggregate run concurrently under a bounded concurrency limit while declared dependencies are respected; precommit.full's ex_dna, reach.check, and dialyzer.json are independent of each other and must no longer run strictly serially
Each gate's stdout and stderr are captured to its own per-run log file; terminal output is a status table of gate, status, duration, and log path rather than interleaved streams
A machine-readable summary maps each gate to its status, duration, and log path, so a reviewer records the checks block from structured data instead of prose about a hand-rolled mktemp path
The existing alias names remain the entry points and behave the same from a caller's view; the aggregate exits non-zero when any gate that is not marked allow-failure fails
Tests cover dependency ordering, concurrent execution of independent gates, failure propagation to the aggregate exit status, and one log file per gate
out_of_scope: Any verdict or judgment logic — the runner counts status, duration, and exit code; the reviewer AI remains the gate and decides what a failure means
Changing which checks belong to which aggregate
Replacing mix aliases as the operator-facing entry point
CI provider configuration — there is no .github/workflows yet and this task does not add one
Retrofitting the log format onto consumer projects' own check commands
task.body:
Two separate documents — this repo's CLAUDE.md ("Capture dispatch-gate output on the first run") and the portfolio harness-workflow include ("Capture dispatch-check output once, to a unique tmp log") — instruct every agent to hand-roll LOG=$(mktemp -t ...) and report the path in the reviewer's checks entry. That is a convention standing in for a mechanism: it depends on each agent remembering, it produces prose instead of data, and it silently fails when an agent forgets and re-runs a verbose gate just to read it.

Separately, precommit.full runs harness.deps.check -> precommit -> ex_dna -> reach.check -> dialyzer.json strictly serially even though the last three are mutually independent, so the pre-PR gate is longer than it needs to be.

Idea from DeepSeek Harness scripts/run-gates.ts: package scripts own the names, the runner owns the graph. Each gate carries {id, label, command, needs, allowFailure}, gates run under bounded in-process parallelism, and each gate's output is captured into its own chunk list instead of being interleaved. The transferable part is the declaration plus captured-log-per-gate plus status table; the closed Mode union and the npm-script plumbing are not.

task.title: Move settled rationale and postmortems out of the eager floor into decision records, with a portable word-ceiling gate
acceptance_criteria: A decision-record tier exists whose path encodes lifecycle (proposed / implemented / rejected) and class, and whose format requires an explicit alternatives-considered section — a decision recorded without what it beat invites the re-litigation the tier exists to prevent

Each settled decision currently narrated inline in CLAUDE.md is represented as a record: the agent-gate workflow ('THE architecture, do not re-litigate'), the build-thin-core orchestration-library choice, and the inline-vs-dispatch routing rule

Postmortems are a separate tier from decision records; the incident narratives currently inline — the 2026-06-12 duplicate-land misread and the backlog-churn observation in the harness-workflow include — move there

CLAUDE.md and priv/includes/harness-workflow.md keep a one-line standing order plus a link per moved item; the behavioral force of every moved rule is unchanged and no standing order loses its imperative

A check validates decision-record format (folder lifecycle agrees with the declared status, required sections present, relative links resolve) and enforces per-file word ceilings from a manifest. The ceiling for the reviewer-facing surface is measured on the RENDERED AGENTS.md, because that is the artifact every cross-family reviewer pays for on every run

The check runs from a clone of this repo without depending on a personal checkout path, and is wired into the pre-PR gate; the current rendered baseline (15,062 words, measured 2026-08-23 after a regen that pulled in new eager critical-rules sections) is recorded in the manifest as the starting ceiling

Ceilings are guardrails, not reduction targets: the failure message names the remedy order (relocate, condense, raise) and raising a ceiling with a stated reason is a legitimate outcome, not a gate bypass
out_of_scope: A mutating auto-regen hook for AGENTS.md — regeneration stays an explicit step and --check stays the gate; a hook that rewrites and re-stages a generated file during a commit is not wanted here
Bilingual or i18n doc pairing
Rewriting the substance of the moved rationale — this is relocation plus a gate, not an edit of the arguments
Trimming the eager floor beyond moving the narrative sections named above
Changing which includes are eager versus load-on-demand
task.body:
CLAUDE.md currently carries three different tiers in one eager-loaded file: standing orders (imperative, must stay ambient), settled-decision rationale ('do not re-litigate' plus the argument that settled it), and incident postmortems (the duplicate-land story, the backlog-churn story). The rationale and the postmortems are the longest passages and the least load-bearing per session — but they are eager, and AGENTS.md is generated from them, so every cross-family reviewer on every run pays for them. Measured 2026-08-23: the rendered AGENTS.md is 15,062 words — and it grew ~1,000 words during the very session that measured it, purely from upstream edits to an eager include, without anyone in this repo touching CLAUDE.md. The file has already been hand-trimmed twice (2026-05-30, 2026-06-22) and grown back both times, which is the argument for a gate rather than a third trim.

Idea from DeepSeek Harness: .agents/notes uses {lifecycle}/{class}/date-title.md with a mandatory '## Alternatives considered' section and a machine-checked format, kept deliberately separate from docs/postmortem (incidents, written only when a bug is subtle AND systemic AND costly to rediscover). docs/AGENTS.md adds per-file word ceilings from a manifest with the stated policy that a too-low ceiling is a budget bug, not a mandate to cut. Skipping their archive tier and their bilingual pairing machinery — dsh-scale ceremony for a problem this repo does not have.

Note on the check's home: sync-agents-md.sh currently lives in a personal marketplace checkout, so the freshness gate is not runnable from a clone. This task's check must be portable; making the existing --check portable is the natural place to fix that.

task.title: Create the harness_agent_adapter package — move the AgentAdapter subsystem into its own repo
acceptance_criteria: A new repo/package exists (mix.exs, README, LICENSE, formatter/credo/dialyzer config, a check alias) holding the subsystem verbatim: lib/harness/agent_adapter.ex (621 LOC) + the 16 modules under lib/harness/agent_adapter/ (1,928 LOC) — behaviour, invoke/2, attach_rules/2, Driver, Watchdog, RulesInjection, Registry, OsProcess, the structs, and the six CLI adapters (claude/codex/cursor/grok/antigravity/pi)

The package's own test suite is green and self-contained: the 20 test/harness/agent_adapter/* files, test/support/agent_adapter/conformance_case.ex, and the fake adapters (fake_adapter.ex, fake_model_adapter.ex, noncompliant_adapter.ex) move with it; ConformanceCase is part of the package's public test surface so a downstream consumer can run it against its own adapters

The package names nothing from harness: no Harness.Run.*, no Harness.AgentRules, no Harness.Worktree, no Harness.Config. Verified by grep plus a clean compile in a checkout that has no harness dependency

The package's public API is written down (module list + the caller-supplied rule-content and watchdog seams that tasks 327/328 created), so harness and Personas OS both program against a named contract rather than against internals
Nothing is deleted from harness in this task — harness keeps compiling against its in-repo copy until the consuming task lands
out_of_scope: Any change inside the harness repo (the sibling consuming task owns that)
Publishing to hex.pm — a git or path dependency is enough to prove the boundary; a hex release can follow once the API has settled
Wiring Personas OS to the package
Changing adapter behaviour, the rule-injection contract, or the watchdog semantics — this is a move, not a redesign
task.body:
Supersedes task 329 (the decision spike): the extraction decision is settled — it is a go. Personas OS (~/_DATA/code/personas, DESIGN.md §5/§8) is the named second consumer; it needs the uniform-Ports driver for the six headless coding-agent CLIs without harness's Run/worktree/lander machinery. No further go/no-go document is required.

Tasks 327 and 328 already did the hard part: the rule-content seam is inverted (the subsystem no longer names Harness.AgentRules) and the Driver -> Run.Reflex -> Worktree.Isolation -> AgentAdapter cycle is broken (the watchdog is a leaf module, Isolation.validate/3 takes its inputs from the caller). The subsystem is therefore dependency-clean, and this task is a mechanical move plus new-repo scaffolding, not a refactor.

Size: 2,549 lib LOC and roughly 2,768 test LOC move; about 5% of harness's lib surface.

Hand-build rather than dispatch: creating the repo and its remote is an operator-gated step, and the work lands in a repo that does not exist yet, so a harness worktree dispatch cannot perform it.

task.title: harness consumes harness_agent_adapter as a dependency — delete the in-repo AgentAdapter subsystem
acceptance_criteria: mix.exs takes the harness_agent_adapter dependency (git or path is acceptable) and lib/harness/agent_adapter.ex plus the whole lib/harness/agent_adapter/ directory are deleted from harness — harness's lib LOC drops by about 2,549

Every caller is repointed at the package namespace: 38 lib files outside the subsystem reference AgentAdapter today, concentrated in agent_registry.ex (17 references), run/actions/worktree.ex (8), audit_review.ex (6), run/result.ex, run/actions/reviewing.ex, dispatch.ex, chat/claude.ex (5 each)

The moved tests are deleted from harness; harness keeps only the tests that exercise harness-side behaviour, and test/support/run_case.ex links against the package's fake adapters instead of local copies
Harness-owned pieces stay in harness and still work: Harness.AgentRules (rule content), Harness.AgentRegistry (availability hints), Harness.Run.*, Harness.Worktree.Isolation
mix precommit.full green on the landed base, including the six adapters' conformance tests now run from the package
out_of_scope: Creating the package (task 396)
Changing adapter behaviour, rule injection, or watchdog semantics
Renaming or reshaping the harness-side surfaces that merely alias the package
Publishing the package to hex.pm
task.body:
Second half of the extraction. Once the package exists (task 396), harness stops carrying its own copy: take the dependency, delete lib/harness/agent_adapter.ex and lib/harness/agent_adapter/, and repoint every caller.

The cost of the extraction lives here, not in the move: 38 lib files outside the subsystem name AgentAdapter today, so the alias sweep is the bulk of the diff. It is mechanical and single-repo, which is why this half is dispatchable while task 396 is not.

This is a repo-wide invariant change — dispatch it as a solo wave with nothing landing in parallel, since any sibling land that adds a new AgentAdapter reference after the fork reddens it at landing time.

task.title: Injected agent rules must never be visible in a tracked file while an agent runs the project's checks
acceptance_criteria: No harness-injected rule content is present in any tracked, repo-owned file at any point where an agent could run the project's check command. The codex/pi channel currently prepends a marker block to the repo's tracked AGENTS.md (RulesInjection.install_codex_rules/1) and only restores it on the delivery-commit path, so implementer, reviewer and audit agents all see a modified AGENTS.md while they run checks

The invariant holds for the AUDIT run specifically: Harness.Audit builds its invocation with rule_content (lib/harness/audit.ex:377) and nothing in the audit path calls cleanup_injected_rules/1 — today the only call site is lib/harness/worktree.ex:810. The audit agent runs the project's clean-build/check itself, so harness cannot sequence a strip-then-check; the injection must not be observable in the first place

A regression test proves it with a project fixture that owns a tracked AGENTS.md plus a freshness check comparing AGENTS.md against CLAUDE.md: the check passes while a codex-channel agent is running. A test asserting only that cleanup restores the file afterwards does not satisfy this criterion — the failure happens mid-run, not after

The rule content still reaches codex and pi agents; this is a change of delivery channel or location, not a removal of rule injection. The six adapters still pass Harness.AgentAdapter.ConformanceCase unchanged

The existing run records whose approved_then_found_red was produced by this bug are corrected in Postgres, with the correcting statement and its selection predicate recorded in the task's implemented note. As of 2026-08-23 every populated approved_then_found_red in run_records — 16 of 16, all project bourse, dates 2026-08-14 through 2026-08-22 — carries an AGENTS.md STALE cold_check tail. Records with an independent real failure (two also cite priv/authority/deribit/contract-baselines.json SHA-256 mismatches) keep their fact; only the AGENTS.md-only ones are cleared
mix check.dispatch green plus focused tests for the rule-injection and audit paths
out_of_scope: Changing what the rules say (Harness.AgentRules content) or which languages get which guidance
The Claude (.harness/agent-rules.md), Cursor (.cursor/rules/) and prompt-preamble channels — those write harness-owned or untracked paths and do not collide with a repo's own files
Making the consumer repo's AGENTS.md freshness test tolerant of an injected header — the test is correct and harness is at fault; a workaround in the consumer is the wrong repo
Any change to routing weights, penalties or auto-exclusion based on approved_then_found_red — routing surfaces the fact and applies no penalty, and that stays true
Reviewer-family or implementer/reviewer pairing rules
task.body:
harness poisons its own reviewer-reliability ledger, and has been doing so since at least 2026-08-14.

The mechanism, verified end to end. RulesInjection.install_codex_rules/1 delivers rules to codex and pi by prepending a marker block plus a separator to the repo's tracked AGENTS.md, merging the repo's own content below it. cleanup_injected_rules/1 restores the file correctly — but its only call site is Worktree.commit's staging path (lib/harness/worktree.ex:810). Between injection and delivery-commit the tracked AGENTS.md is modified, and that is exactly the window in which every agent runs the project's checks.

Consumer repos gate on this file. bourse's test/mix/tasks/ccxt_agents_md_test.exs:407 ("the committed tree is currently fresh") asserts AgentsMd.check("CLAUDE.md", "AGENTS.md", ...) returns :ok against the working tree; the portfolio harness-workflow include actively recommends wiring sync-agents-md.sh --check into the check_command, so any repo following that advice inherits the same fault.

The damage lands in the wrong ledger. Harness.Audit builds its invocation with rule_content (lib/harness/audit.ex:377) into a deliberately un-warmed worktree; the audit agent runs the clean check, sees AGENTS.md drift, and writes cold_check.passed = false. witness_cold_check then records approved_then_found_red on the APPROVED RUN — charging a false approval to the run's reviewer for a file the AUDIT agent's own injection modified. The reviewer never saw it.

Evidence, 2026-08-23, all 16 populated approved_then_found_red rows in run_records:
- 16 of 16 are project bourse, dated 2026-08-14 to 2026-08-22, still accruing
- 16 of 16 carry an AGENTS.md STALE tail. Several audit agents diagnosed it in the artifact themselves: "because harness prepended its ephemeral header", "the harness-injected worktree copy differs from", "harness had injected an uncommitted ephemeral AGENTS.md overlay"
- 2 of 16 additionally cite real deribit contract-baselines.json SHA-256 mismatches — those runs have a genuine finding underneath and must keep it

The cost is not just noise. A peer orchestrator session read this ledger, saw the false approvals concentrate on cursor and grok reviewers, and proposed mechanical family-based blocking of implementer/reviewer pairs — a routing change built on an artifact. Controlling for reviewer identity via reviewer_diff_size (untouched by this bug) shows no family effect at all: intervention is a per-reviewer trait (Codex median 96 lines and 81 percent of runs touched; Cursor 4; Claude 1; Grok 0), and Claude/Opus finds median 0 in the same cursor work that codex rewrites. The bug did not just produce bad numbers, it produced a bad architectural proposal.

Suggested direction, not binding: do not deliver rules by modifying a tracked file at all. When the repo owns an AGENTS.md, route that run's rule content through the prompt-preamble channel instead of merging into the file. Alternatives worth weighing are a nested AGENTS.md at a path the CLI reads but the repo does not track, or an untracked overlay. Whatever is chosen must satisfy criterion 3 — the check has to pass DURING the run, because the agent decides when to run it.
